title: Measure a conversation by turns and uptake
statement: Measure a comprehension conversation by the turns it runs, how much language the learner produces and whether each reply used the learner's answer, not by responses per minute alone.
example: One blueprint treats about five turns as the shape of a comprehension conversation.
detail: The opportunities-to-respond BrainLift's blueprint measures with three signals, not one: responses per minute, turns per conversation and how much language the child produces, along with whether the app actually used the child's answer (`othello-course-renderer-draft/repo/docs/pedagogy/otr-brainlift-2026-07-24.md`, line 106). Following the Strive-for-Five model it treats about five turns as the shape of a comprehension conversation (line 84), and a reply that would read the same whatever the child answered is not a third turn (line 86). Which measures to build, and how to capture young children's spoken answers well enough to score them, it leaves open (line 192).
against: The BrainLift was written for PreK to Grade 2 and calls itself out of scope for grades 3 and above; the Grade 3 course that adopted it treats its age-band specifics as context only (the same file, line 12).

evidence.quote: Measure with three signals, not one: responses per minute, turns per conversation, and how much language the child produces, along with whether the app actually used the child’s answer.
the app should treat about five turns as the shape of a comprehension conversation
A reply that would read the same no matter what the child answered is not a third turn.
The open questions to work through are which of these measures to build into the app, and how to capture a young child’s spoken responses reliably enough to score them.

citations.ref: Cabell & Zucker 2024, Using Strive-for-Five conversations to strengthen language comprehension in preschool through Grade One, The Reading Teacher
